q: Does the exact undirected-graphical-model mapping extend to noisy shallow circuits (depolarizing, amplitude/phase damping, or realistic hardware noise models), and if so does the treewidth stay bounded by min(O(d*l), O(n)) once the Kraus operators are folded into the TN?
basis: Paper is strictly noiseless (pure states, unitary gates). Section 5 caveat (i) in this replication flags noisy-circuit extension as unattempted. Modern supremacy-verification and near-term hardware simulation live in the noisy regime; whether the graphical-model complex-factor picture survives noise Kraus channels (which double each qubit index -> potentially quadruples per-node bond dim) is not obvious a priori.
next_steps: 1) Extend src/tn_sim.py to accept per-qubit / per-2Q-gate Kraus ops, doubling the wire index (physical + auxiliary). 2) Reproduce the C1 correctness check by comparing TN density-matrix contraction to full-Liouville-space evolution on n<=10 with depolarizing p in {0.001, 0.01, 0.05}. 3) Refit the log2(FLOPs) vs depth slope; test whether the slope scales as ~2*l_min (quadratic Liouville-space cost) as expected. 4) Report any regime where noise causes early treewidth blowup vs the noiseless bound.

q: How does the paper's undirected-graphical-model / QuickBB pipeline compare, on identical circuits and identical hardware, against modern tensor-network-contraction benchmarks (cotengra hyper-optimized contraction, quimb slicing, qFlex Feynman-path, and hybrid Schrodinger-Feynman a la Markov+Fatima+Boixo 2018 or Huang et al. 2020)?
basis: Section 5 caveat (iii) in this replication: no comparison against alternative low-depth simulators was made. The 2017 paper predates cotengra (2020, Gray & Kourtis) and hyper-optimized slicing; any 'state-of-the-art classical simulator' claim in 2026 must be re-benchmarked against those.
next_steps: 1) Port our test circuits (5x9 depth 12, 7x7 depth 10, 6x6 depth 10) to quimb + cotengra with hyper-optimizer budget of ~10 min per circuit. 2) Compare largest-intermediate-tensor, total FLOPs, wall-clock, and (for slicing methods) memory footprint against our opt_einsum greedy path AND against the paper's reported QuickBB numbers. 3) Report a head-to-head table on 6-8 circuit sizes. 4) Identify the regime (depth, geometry) in which the 2017 approach still wins vs where cotengra/quimb dominate.

q: Can ML-boosted / learned approximate inference on the graphical-model side (loopy belief propagation with amplitude corrections, neural-network amplitude estimators, or diffusion-model samplers over the elimination order) beat exact variable elimination on the paper's regime while keeping controlled approximation error?
basis: The paper insists on exact inference (variable elimination) because the factors are complex-valued and interference makes naive approximate inference unstable. But recent work (2022-2024) on complex-valued belief propagation, neural tensor-network contraction (Liao+Poulin 2022), and GNN-based elimination-order search (Meirom et al. 2022; Kadavath 2024) offers a candidate approximate path. Whether these can achieve controlled additive error on the amplitude for shallow noise-free supremacy circuits is open.
next_steps: 1) Implement complex loopy BP on the same TN graph and measure |BP_amp - exact_amp| / |exact_amp| vs iteration count on our 70-config sweep. 2) Train a small GNN to predict elimination orderings, compare largest-intermediate against opt_einsum-greedy and against a QuickBB-budget-limited baseline. 3) Compute error-vs-FLOP tradeoff curves; declare the approach viable only if there is a regime where approx error stays <1e-3 with sub-exponential-in-treewidth cost.

q: Does the graphical-model formulation give a useful primitive for sampling-based quantum-supremacy verification (linear cross-entropy benchmark computation) at scales beyond what direct amplitude computation can handle?
basis: The paper computes individual amplitudes exactly. Supremacy verification (Arute et al. 2019; Boixo et al. 2018) needs the marginal cross-entropy over ~1e6 samples, which is O(1e6) amplitude evaluations. The paper doesn't discuss whether their contraction machinery can be reused (shared elimination order, amortized precomputation of upstream tensors) across many bitstrings x for a fixed U.
next_steps: 1) On our sweep, precompute the network for U=|0><0| with all output-wire tensors as *symbolic* rank-2 identity-projectors, then substitute per-bitstring <x| at the leaves. 2) Measure wall-clock per additional bitstring after the first (target: <<1x the first-amplitude cost). 3) If amortization succeeds, extrapolate to a 5x9 depth 12 circuit and estimate whether XEB over 1e5 samples is feasible on a single workstation. 4) Cross-check against Google's 2019 XEB numbers on Sycamore-like small subcircuits.

q: Does the treewidth-boundedness argument extend to circuit topologies with hierarchical / long-range structure such as MERA-like layered ansaetze, brickwork circuits with occasional swaps, or measurement-based quantum-computation cluster states?
basis: The paper's min(O(d*l), O(n)) bound relies critically on 2D nearest-neighbor connectivity: each layer only adds edges between adjacent qubits, so treewidth grows at most linearly in depth. For MERA (which has log-depth logical connectivity via renormalization steps) or MBQC (which starts from a fixed cluster state and uses measurement-adapted single-qubit ops), the graph structure is fundamentally different and the paper's bound is not obviously applicable.
next_steps: 1) Implement MERA circuit generator on n=16 qubits with 4 renormalization levels; measure contraction width and compare against d*l bound. 2) Implement brickwork-plus-random-SWAP circuits with SWAP density 0.05, 0.15, 0.30; identify at which density the treewidth starts to jump. 3) Build 2D cluster-state + measurement-adapted 1Q circuits; measure treewidth as a function of cluster geometry. 4) For each case, report whether an analogous but modified scaling bound (perhaps min(O(d*log l), O(n)) for MERA) fits, or whether the graphical-model approach is fundamentally not tight for these topologies.
